title: Two Clocks, No Federal Rule: Canadian Dock Detention Before Holiday Peak
summary: Canada has no federal detention free-time rule. Set appointment clocks, watch HOS on-duty time, and plan DC labour risk before holiday peak.
body_markdown:
A dry van books a 14:00 appointment into a Greater Toronto Area grocery DC in mid-November. The driver arrives at 13:40 and sits in the yard until 16:10 before a door opens. The rate confirmation says two hours of free time. Someone will argue about whether the clock started at the appointment, at check-in, or when the dock was ready. That argument is still a commercial fight.


The harder problem is already on the ELD. Under Canada's Commercial Vehicle Drivers Hours of Service Regulations, waiting before and while a vehicle is loaded or unloaded counts as on-duty time. South of latitude 60°N, driving caps at 13 hours in a day and must stop after 14 hours of on-duty time, or after 16 hours have elapsed since the last stretch of at least 8 consecutive hours off duty. Three hours in that yard cannot be spent on the next leg. If the outbound load was planned tight, the miss is not a detention invoice. It is a failed pickup, a layover, or an hours-of-service problem waiting to happen.


Canada does not have a federal motor-carrier rule that sets free time, detention rates, or dock-dwell limits. Free time is contractual. The federal clock that actually bites is hours of service. Peak season stacks both clocks on top of DC labour risk that operators in Quebec just watched play out for nearly six months.


## What Canada regulates (and what it leaves to the contract)


Detention and demurrage language gets borrowed from U.S. practice and from ocean and rail tariffs, which is why the terms blur. For highway truckload into a Canadian dock, three facts matter more than the labels:


1.


**There is no federal free-time statute for truck detention at shipper and receiver facilities.** Transport Canada and the National Safety Code set driver hours, vehicle safety, and related carrier duties. They do not prescribe how many minutes a receiver owes before an accessorial starts, or what it pays. Those terms live in the rate confirmation, carrier agreement, or shipper routing guide.


2.


**Waiting is on-duty time.** The federal Hours of Service Regulations include waiting before and while a commercial vehicle is serviced, loaded, unloaded, or dispatched, and waiting before and while the vehicle or its load is inspected. That definition is current to Sept 21, 2026, and last amended June 12, 2021 (SOR/2005-313).


3.


**The duty reaches past the carrier.** Section 4 says no motor carrier, shipper, consignee, or other person shall request, require, or allow a driver to drive out of compliance. A receiver that holds a driver past the point where the next legal move is impossible creates regulatory exposure the carrier, and potentially the shipper or consignee, share.


Ocean and rail demurrage or per diem are different clocks, set by terminals, railways, and shipping lines under their own tariffs. Some railway incidental charges in multi-shipper tariffs can be challenged at the Canadian Transportation Agency under section 120.1 of the Canada Transportation Act. None of that substitutes for a federal truck-detention free-time rule at a grocery DC in Vaughan or Anjou. If your team is waiting for Ottawa to "set detention," you are waiting for a rule that does not exist.


## Why this week and the next eight matter


October through December is when Canadian retail and grocery inbound calendars compress. Appointment portals fill earlier. Live-unload windows get narrower. Night and weekend labour coverage becomes the difference between a door that turns and a yard that stacks. That is a dock-capacity and labour story, not a spot-rate story.


Two recent data points set the tone for fall 2026:


-


**Labour supply in the broader sector is up, not collapsing.** Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey put transportation and warehousing employment at 1,119,200 in September 2026, up 52,800 (5.0%) from September 2025, after a small month-over-month dip of 1,200 from August (The Daily tables published Oct 9, 2026). Growth does not mean every DC door is staffed for November. The failure mode is uneven coverage and appointment discipline.


-


**Truck transportation vacancies remain elevated versus the all-industry average.** An industry labour tracker drawing on Statistics Canada job-vacancy tables reported a Q2 2026 vacancy rate of 4.8% in truck transportation versus 3.1% across all industries, with 13,780 vacant transport-truck-driver positions that quarter (tables 14-10-0442-01 and 14-10-0443-01, September 2026). Drivers who burn hours in yards are harder to put back on the next retail load.


Industrial space is tightening as peak freight arrives. A national industrial market survey for Q3 2026 put Canada's overall industrial availability at 5.2%, down 30 basis points from the prior quarter, with about 10.3 million square feet of net absorption, the strongest quarterly total since late 2022. Toronto held near 5.0% availability. Montreal fell to 6.3%. Calgary sat near 3.6%. When warehouse space thins in the corridors that move grocery and retail freight, receivers have less room to stage late arrivals. The overflow lands on carrier equipment and the appointment board.


## The Quebec produce DC reminder


From March 30 to September 24, 2026, a strike at a produce distribution centre in Laval, Quebec, plus related transportation and head-office units, kept roughly 550 unionized workers off the job. Public reporting in early April described empty produce shelves at stores supplied by that network, covering hundreds of grocery locations across Quebec. A tentative agreement landed September 17. Workers ratified on September 24. Gradual resumption was set for September 27.


That was not a detention dispute. It was a labour failure mode that removed a receiving and outbound engine for nearly six months. Carriers and brokers on those lanes lived the downstream version: cancelled appointments, redirected freight, contingency cross-docks, and customers who still expected windows to hold. Peak season does not need another multi-month strike to hurt. A short-staffed afternoon shift at a GTA or Montreal grocery DC produces the same pile-up in a day. DC labour belongs on the Q4 load plan, not in the background.


## Decision 1: Define the detention clock in writing, then stop arguing about folklore


Because federal law will not define free time for you, your documents have to. For every recurring Canadian receiver that generates dwell, decide and publish:


-


When free time starts (appointment time, gate check-in, or dock assignment)


-


How long free time runs (and whether live load and drop-and-hook differ)


-


What evidence is required (gate timestamp, dock-in, dock-out, POD notes, geofence, appointment confirmation)


-


Notice rules (how soon the carrier must flag detention while still on site)


-


Who pays when the shipper caused the delay versus when the receiver did


-


Whether a late truck keeps the original window, joins a standby queue, or must rebook


If free time starts at arrival, early trucks burn the window in the yard. If it starts at the appointment, late trucks eat their own time. Both are legitimate commercial choices. Leaving the choice implicit is how every November invoice turns into a January dispute.


## Decision 2: Plan the HOS clock first, the accessorial second


Detention pay does not restore driving time. A carrier that "wins" three hours of detention and loses the next pickup has not won. Build schedules that assume realistic dwell at named facilities, not the free-time number on the rate confirmation.


-


Tag high-dwell receivers and protect buffer before the next appointment.


-


Refuse or reprice same-day live dual stops into known afternoon congestion unless remaining on-duty time covers the plan.


-


Treat a missed appointment that forces a next-day rebook as a root-caused service failure (labour, yard, carrier late, weather), not a default carrier fault.


-


Remember section 4. Pushing a driver to "just make the next window" after a multi-hour hold is how a commercial delay becomes a compliance problem.


Asset fleets feel this in payroll and missed revenue miles. Brokers feel it when the replacement truck is a day later and the customer still expects the original ETA. Hybrids feel both when the private fleet burns hours at a preferred DC and the brokerage arm covers the overflow.


## Decision 3: Treat DC labour risk as a routing input


The Laval dispute showed how one produce DC can reshape inbound and outbound patterns for a provincial network. You do not need perfect labour intelligence. You need a short list of facilities where a staffing miss breaks your week, and a cover plan for each.


-


Rank top receivers by dwell hours and revenue concentration for Q4.


-


Ask shippers which DCs cap appointments by door and shift, and which still run first-come queues dressed up as appointments.


-


For grocery and retail peak, book further ahead than the portal's minimum. Peak fills the calendar before it fills the yard.


-


Keep an alternate cross-dock or secondary DC path for perishable and promotional freight where a one-day miss becomes a dump or a chargeback.


Shippers and 3PLs that control the dock have the cleanest lever: align inbound appointments to actual labour, not theoretical door count. Carriers cannot staff the receiver's night shift. They can stop accepting appointments the facility cannot execute.


## Decision 4: Separate ocean or rail demurrage fights from highway detention fights


Drayage teams in Montreal, Vancouver, and Halifax already juggle terminal storage, railway per diem, and line-owned container detention. Those charges have tariffs and, for some railway incidental items, an Agency complaint path. Highway live-unload detention at a DC does not. Mixing the clocks in one dispute file is how finance pays the wrong bill. Keep container equipment clocks and power-unit dwell clocks in different claim types, with different evidence packs.


## Encoding this in the workflow


Every freight business has a different mix of grocery DCs, retail windows, drop-and-hook ratios, and rebook tolerance. A generic "two-hour detention" rule copied from a U.S. playbook will not match a Prairie grain receiver, a GTA grocery live unload, or a Montreal cross-dock feeding store delivery. The shops that bleed less in Q4 are the ones whose statuses, permissions, and billing fields already match how they run.


-


**Hard fields at appointment status.** Facility, appointment start, free-time rule, clock-start rule, and required evidence, so a load cannot sit in "delivered" with a detention claim and no timestamps.


-


**Facility-level dwell profiles.** Gate-to-dock and dock-to-release for the receivers that matter, refreshed after peak.


-


**HOS-aware dispatch gates.** A warning when remaining on-duty time cannot cover planned dwell plus transit to the next stop.


-


**Accessorial approval paths that match money flow.** Who can authorize detention toward the shipper, who can promise it to the carrier, and what document closes the claim.


-


**Labour-disruption flags on facilities.** A status that blocks or re-prices tenders when a DC is on strike, short-staffed, or on contingency hours.


When those rules reflect how a specific shop sells service and pays carriers, detention becomes a controlled exception instead of a spreadsheet fight. That is the point of configuring workflows around a unique book of business, not a template.


## What to do this week


-


Pull the last 90 days of Canadian live-unload stops and rank facilities by average dwell and by detention dollars actually collected, not just billed.


-


Rewrite free-time language for the top ten receivers before November appointments lock.


-


Add remaining on-duty time to the dual-stop check in dispatch, with a hard stop when the math does not work.


-


Confirm which grocery and retail DCs you touch have door-and-shift appointment caps versus open calendars.


-


Write a one-page cover plan for each high-concentration DC: alternate facility, cross-dock, or deferral rule if labour or appointments break.


-


Train billing and ops on the difference between highway detention evidence and container demurrage or per diem evidence.


Holiday peak will not wait for a federal detention rule that is not coming. The operators who protect margin and service will treat appointments, on-duty time, and DC labour as one plan.


## FAQ


### Does Canada have a federal truck detention free-time rule?


No. Free time and detention rates at shipper and receiver docks are set by contract. Federal rules regulate hours of service and related safety duties, not dock detention tariffs.


### Does waiting at a Canadian dock count against hours of service?


Yes. The Commercial Vehicle Drivers Hours of Service Regulations include waiting before and while a vehicle is loaded, unloaded, serviced, or dispatched as on-duty time, which feeds the daily 13-hour driving and 14-hour on-duty limits south of latitude 60°N.


### Can a shipper or receiver share hours-of-service exposure?


Yes. Section 4 of the regulations prohibits a motor carrier, shipper, consignee, or other person from requesting, requiring, or allowing a driver to drive out of compliance, so holding a driver into an illegal next move is not only the carrier's problem.


### Why is fall 2026 a sharper detention risk in Canada?


Retail and grocery appointment calendars compress in Q4, industrial availability tightened again in Q3 2026 in a national market survey (to about 5.2%), and operators are coming off a nearly six-month produce DC labour disruption in Laval that showed how facility labour can reshape inbound freight.


### Is transportation and warehousing employment falling in Canada?


Not on the latest Labour Force Survey read. Employment in the sector was 1,119,200 in September 2026, up 5.0% year over year, even after a small August-to-September dip.


### Should detention pay be the main fix for long dwell?


No. Detention may recover some cost, but it does not restore driving time or save the next appointment. The higher-leverage fixes are facility-specific free-time rules, HOS-aware scheduling, and appointment capacity that matches real labour.
